claims.text: Simultaneous reduction of all metal precursors promotes concurrent nucleation.
Concurrent nucleation drives formation of homogeneously alloyed noble metal–based high-entropy nanoparticles.
Simultaneous precursor reduction mitigates phase separation and elemental segregation.
The proposed initial state is a homogeneous, stoichiometrically consistent mixture of noble-metal precursors in solution or on a support.
Rapid, controlled heating under a reductive atmosphere can force nearly simultaneous reduction of the metal precursors.
Fine temperature control in a controlled reducing environment minimizes differences in reduction kinetics among the metal species.
Synchronized reduction produces temporal overlap among nucleation events.
Overlapping nucleation events cause metal atoms to coalesce into nanoparticles before diffusion produces segregation.
Concurrent reduction and nucleation facilitate uniform incorporation of the different metals into individual nanoparticles.
Staggered reduction allows an early-reducing metal to nucleate first, causing phase separation or uneven subsequent growth.
Synchronized reduction will yield more compositionally uniform nanoparticles than an otherwise unchanged conventional-heating baseline.
Synchronized reduction will improve nanoparticle morphology control relative to the baseline.
Synchronized reduction will enhance surface-atom exposure relative to the baseline.
Standard synthesis without engineered kinetic synchronization typically produces heterogeneous structures, phase-separated regions, or elemental segregation.
The proposed mechanism applies particularly to reductive nanoparticle syntheses containing five or more interacting metals.
The mechanism may not apply when precursor reduction behaviors are extremely disparate or when nanoparticle formation is non-reductive.
The proposed comparison holds precursor mixture and other synthesis parameters constant while changing the heating protocol intended to synchronize reduction.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in compositional uniformity, morphology control, or phase-separation suppression is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.
